utterances.text: I know that. I heard that these units existed, that they were on Santiceva Street, even though from among the men who were there, I did not know any. You should know that at that point, for the prisoners it was not important whose unit it was, or at least to me it was not important. That was not that important. What was important was to just stay alive, to survive. And as to who was forcing you to work, who was shooting, that was a side matter. And I could have been killed either by a bullet that would come from behind or from a bullet that would come from the ABiH that were in front of us. It was a nightmare. I don't know, but for instance, I heard about this Solaja. And whether he was under Tuta, too, or not, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, while you were there at Santiceva Street in those three or four days, did you ever eyewitness any detainees getting killed or injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I experienced that. I think it was on the third or fourth day -- the fourth day was hellish, at least while I was there, from the rumour, I was, from my cellblock [as interpreted]. I think over 30 of us were taken to Santiceva Street. And over 20 men were wounded, and a fellow inmate was killed at that time. But that night was hell. Many, many were wounded. It so happened that I was not. I prayed to God that night to -- rather have me killed, so that I would not be disabled. But this Zuka was killed. It was a man who was about 30 years of age. His last name was Zukanovic, and he was in my room. We pulled him out, and then he was taken somewhere, I don't know where. When we reached the area behind that car, he was already dead. We were repairing a parapet, and we were supposed to push the car a little bit ahead some 5 metres. And he just knelt down and fell. Another fellow prisoner and I pulled him out. It was hard for us to pull him out because he was fairly big. And then they took him either to the hospital or the morgue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you, you described this day as particularly hellish. Why was it worse than the other days at Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't know why it was worse. Probably because there was some kind of operation that had us go to move the line. I don't know. But that day, in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I object to the witness purely guessing and speculating now. I don't think it's proper for the witness, a fact witness, to speculate and guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, in your testimony, you have to tell us what you saw and what is your recollections, rather than what you heard and guessed. Yes, you may continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Compared to what you experienced that day, why was it worse than the other days? And just describe the situation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't know why it was worse, but that day, it was a real war. It was hell. Why that happened, I have no idea. But that day was unbearable. Those who lived through it, and I myself, the next day, I saw that I just couldn't stand on my feet. I think that I was mentally gone, or that day my blood pressure shot up. But I don't know what the purpose of that was. I know that it was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just testified before that you saw this man named Tuta at the Ero Hotel. Was that the same day as the day you described now, or was it a few days before or after this particular day you've just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That was before, I think a couple of days before. But not at the Hotel Ero. We were not allowed to go into the hotel. It was strictly forbidden to us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The basement of the hotel, I mean. That's what you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. It was a day earlier, day before. But not that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, were you ever assigned to any other tasks than working at the confrontation lines? Did you do any other sort of labour as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of other work did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I did everything, from the front line, to apartment looting, house plundering, removing everything that people used to own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've said that you looted apartments. How many times did you do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I went several times. It was always different people who went. I went several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for which group of soldiers did you have to do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I've no idea what group of soldiers it was. But I did that. They were military. They would come to the camp, pick us up, and take us, and we wouldn't know where -- whether we were being taken to dig trenches or make bunkers or carry furniture out of other people's flats. It's only when they bring you to a place that you see what you are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the map is still on the overhead projector. Could you indicate the areas in Mostar, or if it was in Mostar, and if you can indicate it, where you actually had to loot houses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you need to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Next to the northern entrance into the Velez stadium, there is a settlement, a locality there, and that is where we did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate it on the map, and maybe put a mark with an "L" next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that occasion, did you recognise any of the soldiers who were there with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: You mean those who forced us to do that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Personally, those soldiers who came to get us from the camp, who took us to loot those flats, I did not know them personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who were there present at the flat, not -- did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: In that flat -- it was only downstairs. While we were doing a job, we would go in with two soldiers, and they would tell us what we were to take out and load on to trucks. And once, and again, I'm saying this with a reservation, I once saw Mr. Martinovic downstairs with some soldiers, although that same gentleman did not issue any orders to us or communicated with us in any way what he was doing with those soldiers. Whether it was under him or not, I do not know that. But we had to load all those things, and those were mostly things of some value. We had to load them into a truck, and we did not then go with that truck to unload it. We had to wait for another truck to come up. Where this was unloaded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been referring to a man name -- you called Mr. Martinovic. Did you know this man from before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I knew Martinovic by sight. We were not acquainted. I mean, we were never introduced to one another, but I knew him by sight. I mean, I knew him. I knew who he was, although I had never any contact with him or any...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These apartments that you looted, were these apartments that belonged to Muslim people? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: All Muslim, I do not know. This is an assumption again. But I suppose that was the case. I did not see many nameplates on doors. Mostly there was nobody in those flats. They were abandoned, no owners, or anyone. These flats had been vacated. And we took things from those flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, a little bit earlier on in your testimony, you said that you also worked at the Studenski Dom. What is it that you had to do there, and for how many days did you work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I can say that the quietest few days of all my days in the camp was at the students' hostel, those two or three days. Nobody beat me there, nobody harassed me there. That was the only time in camp when I wished I would go to the students' hostel the next day, too. I and a group of others were there, we were about 10 there. And we prepared beds there for Croat troops and carrying beds upstairs and placing around, arranging six to eight beds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many beds you mounted in that -- in those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I think we put together about 200 beds - couldn't be less - in those few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had to mount these beds for Croat troops. How did you know that, that these beds were meant for Croat troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I knew it because I talked with those people. There was already a group of them there. And I even talked with a man from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Croat soldiers were already there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know how many soldiers exactly. I cannot say that because I could have no knowledge of that. But there must have been 30, 40. But I just don't know. I can't say exactly. But they were there. I saw them, and I talked with those people. There was one from Split, from Osijek -- from Osijek, and they even gave me cigarettes. I sat down with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The map is still on the overhead projector. Could you indicate the area where this Studenski Dom is located in Mostar, maybe if you could put them...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you can put an "S" next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've talked about Tuta's unit. Do you know any member of Tuta's unit personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I personally know -- I knew him well before the war. And his name is Kemo Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how come that -- how did you know him? How were you acquainted to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: We knew one another before the war because we lived in the same neighbourhood, and his brother was my school fellow. I simply knew him from before the war. I also know his father well. He had a shop in the old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see this Kemo whilst you were detained at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did see him at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No. Once I had just been brought to the Heliodrom, and they were taking me for some interrogation -- or rather, to another building. And I was walking with two other men. He came towards me, and he stopped to -- and asked me if I needed any cigarettes or something. And I said no, thank you. And that was when I saw him, but that was just in passing, just a fleeting moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing at that time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: A uniform. A uniform, and he had a pistol. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this man Kemo Selmanovic, what's his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later find out that this Mr. Selmanovic also visited your wife and your brother-in-law at the time that you were in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your wife tell you about that visit -- or I don't know if there were more visits than just one. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: He was on friendly terms with my wife's brother so that as my wife told me, came several times and would stay there, would sit there for a while. On several occasions, he came -- she told me. I'm telling you what I heard. I did not see that, and this is what my wife told me. Once he came and -- well, I don't know what state he was in. But he was there, and he showed to them a handful of keys, saying that he had driven out those Muslims that day or the day before, that is, he bragged about it. He seemed to take pride in the -- in this fact, in having driven several families from their homes. And that same Kemo, I suppose my family was driven out sometime in October. And I believe that he, since my family was with my brother's wife's family, that is, they were together in one flat, I think that is what they are assuming, too, that Kemo had helped them to stay there longer than others, even though that wasn't much help really. Perhaps it would have been better for them had they been driven earlier. But they were among the last to be driven across to the left bank, I mean my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe let's just talk about what happened to your wife and your children, because what did they do after you were taken to the Heliodrom? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: They stayed at my brother's for another two or three days, but it wasn't really particularly good so that my wife decided to go back to our flat. But when she got there, she hardly found anything there. I mean, things were gone, furniture was gone. There was nowhere to lie down. But she was there for a while, for about a fortnight or so. And then she was chased out of there, too. That is, they came one day and expelled her from it, and it was only then that she went to her mother's, to Avenija, so that she had to leave the flat. And she never went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they came, and then she had to leave her apartment, who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Well, according to what she says, a soldier, a military came. But she wasn't -- she found that out later, because later on, she went there, she spent some time around and found out that man who was in Mostar but that he came originally from Konjic. I don't know his name or anything. But be that as it may, that man moved into our flat which was practically empty. How long he lived there, I don't know, not long probably because he could not do that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife find out from which army this soldier was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't -- I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that she then moved to her mother's place. Now, where did her mother live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Her mother lived on Rudarska Street, near the old Velez pitch. It used to be Rudarska Kolonija. Minus colony now. I don't know what it's called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've already touched upon it a little bit, but what happened in October in that year, 1993, to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes. You mean when they were expelled?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please describe how this happened and who expelled them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Well, I'm again telling you what I heard, if you will accept that. They were expelled in late October, and then two or three men came. But there was a neighbour of theirs there who had -- who entered the house directly and told them they had to leave, they had to cross the river. That fellow -- but I have to go back. My children were brought up at my mother-in-law's place so that my daughter, especially my older daughter knew that man well. And he was Solaja, and they used to play together when they were little children. But he was ruthless, they had to leave, they had to leave that apartment, my wife, my children, mother-in-law, my brother-in-law, his wife, his children. Now, the problem was that my younger daughter was not there because she was playing somewhere outside or was visiting somebody. I don't know. At any rate, she wasn't there, and so my wife started crying and saying, "Well, until we find the child, we won't go." But they refused to accept that and took them to Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Well, this one, Solaja. So they expelled them, took them there, they crossed over. What do I know? And he returned. Meanwhile, my youngest daughter had returned to the flat and found nobody there and saw that there was nobody. And of course, she was frightened and didn't know what to do and where to go. So she came down the stairs again to come out and see where everybody was. But this Solaja had returned in the meantime, and they met, and he took her to Bulevar so as to take her to the left bank also. And so he did. And they then met again on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Witness, I'm almost done with my examination-in-chief. There's only one thing I want to look at, which is Exhibit 704.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, there's -- well, maybe if he could first look at the front page and read out the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "The payroll for November 1993. You will found enclosed here with the payroll for the members of the Convicts Battalion for November 1993, anti-terrorist group, commander of the Convicts Battalion, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would first like you to look at the page, and maybe the usher can assist you. I want you to go to page number 00795386. And these numbers are indicated on the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, 00795386. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read out what's written there before the list of names starts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "Defence department, Convicts Battalion" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, underneath that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "Number 022/2-403/93, Siroki Brijeg, 02121993."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, actually what I wanted to know is the next thing which is then written down there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "ATG, Vinko Skrobo."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then move to number 22. Whose name appears there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "Dario Solaja," yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the man you have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, that is him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now go to page number 00795361. And would you again read what's written on the top of it just above the line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "Defence Department, combat group 6."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then read out the name which is under Number 12.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: "Kemo Semanovic".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the person you have been testifying about today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there is five minutes to the break. Are you going to do the cross-examination in the morning session, or prefer to do it in the afternoon, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We would prefer to do it after lunch, Your Honour. Perhaps if we do, it will be much shorter and concise if we can look at our notes during the lunch hour. We would prefer 2.30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, would you please show the witness out of the room after pulling down the blinds. We will resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.57 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness is let back in, I would like to use the opportunity to let you know about the letter with -- this counsel has sent to Dr. Skavic in relation to his opinion. This was the exhibit which was marked as D2/25. I have already furnished the Registry with a copy of the translation and all the correspondence between us, and Dr. Skavic and I have also provided a copy of the sets to the Prosecution before -- during the lunch break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness in. Good afternoon, Witness. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have the ELMO lowered. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Meek:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness AB. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Meek, and I represent one of the -- I am one of the attorneys representing Mr. Naletilic. I have a few questions for you. Is it my understanding that you were arrested and taken into custody on the same date to the Heliodrom, on 19th day of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, you did not get it right. I was taken on the 3rd of July, and my family was expelled from the apartment on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you lived, then, between the 9th day of May, which you -- which date you testified about on your direct examination, and the 3rd day of July when you were taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Between 9 May and 1st of July, I lived in my apartment. We were all together. And then we moved over to my brother's from where I was taken to the camp, and my wife moved back into the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a fact, then, that between 9 May of 1993 and the 3rd day of July, 1993, there were no soldiers coming to your apartment except on one occasion that you testified concerning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: From 9 May to 1 July, they came twice. I already stated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in your direct examination that you were -- had personal contact with an individual named Braco Merdzo, and that you knew him personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I did not say that I had personal contact during my stay at the Santiceva Street, but I knew him and he knew me. But we did not have any contact while I was working on Santiceva Street, or during the breaks. When I would see him, we would not talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I made to understand that you did know this gentleman prior to the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes. I know where he lives -- we simply knew each other for a number of years prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a commander of the military police stationed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I heard that, but I cannot confirm that for you. I don't have a source of information that would allow me to confirm it. I only heard that that is what he was, but that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also hear or did you become aware that this gentleman, Mr. Merdzo, was indicted with four others and tried in Mostar for war crimes whereupon he was acquitted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AB, thank you for your testimony. Thank you for coming. And I wish you the best of luck in the rest of your luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of Vinko Martinovic has no good reason to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- had to mount beds for Croatian troops, were HVO soldiers also wearing uniforms? And if that is the case, how were you able to distinguish between Croatians and HVO? How did you make the difference between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: They had -- I believe they had different insignia. They also had these combat uniforms, but I had contact with them, and they told me that that is where they had come from. I had personal contact with them. But as far as the uniforms are concerned, they were not very different. You could not distinguish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness, for coming here to give us the evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you good luck in your future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have two exhibits, which I would like to tender. One is the photograph 20.9, which was marked by the witness; that's the photograph of the Heliodrom, building at the Heliodrom. And I think it gets the number 20.9/2. Is that correct? And the other exhibit is the little map of Mostar, which the witness made various marks on. And that, I think, will become Exhibit 11.18/10. Those are the two exhibits I'd like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections from Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So they are admitted into the evidence. And Madam Registrar will give each a proper number, I believe. Yes, how about the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The next witness will be examined by Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness who is called to testify now requested the following protective measures: Pseudonym and facial image distortion, and I would say that the situation with this witness is very sensitive. As you may know from his summaries, or his witness statements, he served -- being in Mostar, he served in the HVO. So his situation is very sensitive, and he requested such kind of protective measures, [redacted]. But we cannot rule out the possibility that some day he will travel to Bosnia. So this is my request to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections to those protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Your request for the protective measures is granted. Would you please brief us on the relevance to the indictment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My question will go mostly to background, paragraph 7, 10, 11; superior authority, paragraphs 14 through 17; general allegations, paragraph 18; count 1, paragraphs 26 through 28, 32, 34(a), (b), (d); counts 2 through 8, paragraphs 35 to 38; count 18, paragraph 54; and count 21, paragraph 57. Your Honour, I -- there was a slip of my tongue. I myself disclosed information about the witness. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you prepare a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness will be AC.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Poriouvaev:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sit closer to the microphone. Otherwise we'll not understand each other. Witness, your request for protective measures has been granted by the Trial Chamber. Now you will be called "Witness AC," and your facial image will also be distorted so that the public would not see it on the screen. If you need for some reason to reveal some names of people who are close to you, we should go then into private session. But I shall warn you if we need a private session, and I will request it from the Trial Chamber. Otherwise, you should not pronounce the names of people close, next of kin, for example, your brothers, mother, father, and so on, because their names re also -- should be protected. Is it clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: It's clear. It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AC has fluent English, but he prefers to give his testimony still in his own language, so he will give testimony in B/C/S. Witness, you were born in Mostar 1975 and lived there more or less continuously until November 1993. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that you grew up and lived on the west side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have any relatives living in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AC, have you ever known a person named Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How and when did you get acquainted with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Stela, Vinko Martinovic worked as a taxi driver in Balinovac, and I have known him practically all my life. He lived not far from my home, and in fact, he was on friendly terms with my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he know personally you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will not expound too much on your participation in the war against the Serbs, but I cannot skip this part of your background, just we'll discuss this probably in very general terms, I think. So I am directing you to April 1992 where you were in any way involved with the defence of Mostar against the Serbs. Could you briefly inform the Trial Chamber about this period in your background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, during the defence of Mostar, I started my participation by putting up posters of Ali Izetbegovic and President Tudjman. When the war started, the weapons were distributed and part of the weapons were also in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's agree upon one issue. You should slow down, not to create problems for the interpreters. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Are we ready now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: When the weapons were distributed, part of them were in my house. I took myself a rifle, and I said that nobody can take this rifle away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else from your family participate in the defence of Mostar as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, my brother participated in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which unit did you belong at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: At first, it was the defence of Mostar, and later on, we joined the 4th Battalion Tihomir Misic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during the Serb war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, during the war against the Serbs, I spent that whole period in the Tihomir Misic, 4th Battalion of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you consider during that period of time was the commander, either officially or unofficially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Can you make that question more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Who was your commander within that unit, I mean the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: The very beginning, it was Tihomir Misic, called Tiho. After his death, his father took over, Mladen Misic, nicknamed Dedo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your group commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: At first, it was Vinko Martinovic, called Vina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify this issue now. Just Vinko Martinovic. Is it the same Vinko Martinovic that has the nickname of Stela, or different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: No, it is a different person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay on the confrontation line with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I stayed from the very beginning of the war, and until the beginning of the war between the Muslims and the Croats, which means between a year and a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you still keeping with the front lines in the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the front line. I was at the front line until May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening in Mostar just in the beginning -- in the end of April and in the beginning of May? Did you observe any changes in the situation in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice a number of changes in Mostar. There were even rumours that war would break out between the Muslims and the Croats. I could not believe that because until then, we were standing shoulder to shoulder, and we were jointly defending the city against the same enemy. One of my friends told me that the war would break out, and that he was packing his belongings and moving to the east side of Mostar. I couldn't believe the situation. I just could not even think that what happened between the Croats and Muslims was -- really happened. And I thought that perhaps there would be just a small skirmish or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you just on the eve, let's say, the beginning of the war, the 9th of May? Where did you spend the 8th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I was in a restaurant called Oasa, oasis, that was the gathering place for people with whom I usually spent my time on the front line during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Mario Milicevic, called Baja, was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother was also present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, there was my brother, too, and other members of that group that I belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber about the person whom you called Mario Milicevic or Baja. Did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I've known this person practically all my life. [redacted] [redacted]. That day, he told me -- I mean the 8th of May, he told me that he had to go and have a meeting with my Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, with regard to some conflicts that would be erupting between Muslims and Croats. He said that we were -- that a few hours after his meeting with Tuta, we were to meet in his restaurant, which was called Palm Beach. And that then he will explain to us about that conflict, after his meeting with Tuta, and that he would tell us more about that when we met at the Palm Beach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with him in the second restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, after a while, that is, a few hours later, we met in that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. coffee shop, and Baja explained certain things that were going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he explain to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, he explained, he said that on the 9th of May, war would break out between Muslims and Croats. And that he had to seize our weapons from us, but those were his good soldiers, that he would provide us with full protection. And he even allowed us to go, collect our things, and move over to the east side, or stay where we were and share the fate of the then Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back a little bit to Mario Milicevic, did he occupy any important position in 1992 during the war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Oh, come now, he didn't occupy a really important position. He was just a foot soldier, like I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now you have just mentioned a certain Tuta. Did you hear this name before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes. I kept hearing this name throughout the war, even during the war with the Serbs. And I knew that it was a very dangerous battalion or company or whatever you care to call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at the time his real name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I learned it in the early days of the war between Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Baja explain to you what exactly was being prepared against the Muslims? In Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: No, Baja did not tell us that exactly. What he did say was that something was afoot, that something would happen. But that at two o'clock a.m., he was to meet with Tuta in his restaurant, Palm Beach, and discuss that situation more, and that the measures that had to be taken would be explained to him at that time, that is, at 2.00 a.m. at the meeting with Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he return after the meeting with Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, he returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that meeting about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that around 5.00 in the morning, a war would break out between Muslims and Croats, and that some parts of the city would be cleansed ethnically of Muslims, and that we, being Muslims, could not take part in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Baja propose or advise you of anything since the situation was being deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I've just said it, that Baja offered two possibilities, two solutions for us, for the Muslims. The first alternative was to collect our belongings and cross over to the east side, and the second one was to stand shoulder to shoulder to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I was very young then, so I couldn't really decide by myself. I didn't really quite have a good grasp of the situation. I didn't really know what was going on. So I decided to wait for the decision of Muslims, I mean other Muslims who were in my company, so that we could arrive at the same decision. And our decision was to stay shoulder to shoulder with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you opt to stay with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: At that time, I could not trust anyone. And we were shoulder to shoulder. We defended each other in the war against Serbs. And the situation changed suddenly radically, and the Muslims and Croats suddenly -- so I just couldn't trust anyone, and I thought it would be best, since if I said, well, right, I'm then going across to the other side, then I thought, well, perhaps they will slaughter all my family because they would then think I was a Muslim, though I was a Muslim, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you stay for a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: We stayed in Baja's house. They were there for about three to five days, and he offered full guarantees, that nothing would happen to us and our families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Three to five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you observe in Mostar on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I observed major fighting. I couldn't really see anything because we were in the house. All I could hear was intensive shelling, and there was fierce fighting. One could hear gunfire all around the town. I could hear major detonation which I think came from the direction of Balinovac, when the mosque was mined. And we were scared. We could not do anything on our own. We were just sitting and waiting to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the mosque destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, the mosque was destroyed. It was razed to the ground. It was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was involved in the explosion of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, I could not see who had mined it. I cannot say that I am quite sure about certain things. But from what people said, I learned it was Benito and Kvesic who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to which unit they belonged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the newly formed unit, an ATG unit, Benko Penavic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to Baja in the period of time that you were living in his apartment? Did you -- did he inform you about the events in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, Baja dropped in a couple of times and told us not to be afraid, that everything would be all right, and told us that there was fierce fighting at Rondo, Bulevar, along Santiceva, and in other parts of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- I'm checking the transcript. We have only one name here, Benito, and the other one, who else was involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I think I mentioned those two names already, Benito and Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It was not in the transcript. That's why I asked you again. All right, there came a time when you had to leave Baja's apartment. What was your decision? What were your options?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, Baja said that we would also be his soldiers, that we would be members of the Benko Penavic AT group. He gave us back our weapons and explained to us certain things. And those things were that in -- during his meeting with Tuta, Tuta told him that he did not trust Muslims and did not want any Muslims in his unit. But if Baja trusted those men of his own that much, that then he could admit them into his unit, but if anything happened, that then it could cost Baja his own life. He also explained to us that he did not want to hear any answer, because he did not want any conflict and any difficulty with Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to know, did he tell you anything concrete about the unit? Who were members of the unit, who was the commander? What was the structure of the unit, more or less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I see. He told me that our unit was now a unit under Tuta's authority, that Tuta was number one for those units. He told us that we were to take part in the ethnic cleansing of civilian Muslims in the territory of Mostar and explained to us where our front line was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: It was called elite unit ATG Benko Penavic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what stands for Benko Penavic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, I don't, but I can guess that it is an Ustasha --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: -- from the earlier war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would object to a fact witness such as this guessing. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this witness's testimony now does not touch upon the central part of the indictment as well as the involvement Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of your client. Let's hear the answer from this witness. Witness, you may continue to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, I've answered the question already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Can you then ask it again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just I wanted to know if you know why the unit was named Benko Penavic. Do you know anything about the person whose name was or is Benko Penavic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that person, about Benko Penavic. But as I have already said, I think this is a name of an old Ustasha from the former war, and that that Ustasha was called Benko Penavic, and the unit was named after him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And a little bit about the structure of the unit, Benko Penavic. Yes, my question was to tell me about the structure of the unit. Was it divided into groups, platoons, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, it was divided. There were men who were assigned to the front line to defend the front line, and there were also men whose assignment was to cleanse some parts of the town, I mean ethnically cleanse parts of the town of the Muslim population. The latter were also to participate in all possible operations conducted in different parts of Mostar, and in case of some other dangerous ground, we were to be sent there to resolve whatever problems might be there. And those men were picked out by Baja himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of assignments did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I was one of those who belonged in this platoon, in this company, which was to conduct the ethnic cleansing of the population, to go into all the necessary -- on all the necessary missions, to bring prisoners from Heliodrom, to guard them during their labour duty as they filled the bags with sand and as they worked on the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in the ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what this ethnic cleansing consisting [sic]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: It consisted of -- well, a part of the town is indicated, a borough, a neighbourhood, positions are taken in this neighbourhood, and then you go from one flat to the other, and all the Muslims are thrown out of their flats. These Muslims thrown out of their flats would be loaded onto trucks, some were taken to the Heliodrom, and others would go past the Catholic church and along the Bulevar, and then sent over to the east part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you indicate on the map the locations from where the Muslims were expelled? I mean, first of all locations in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show our witness Exhibit Number 11.18. You may take the pointer, the marker. First you should explain and then encircle the area, the relevant area, from where the Muslims were expelled. Of course, I understand that the names of the streets have changed and even the names of some districts have changed. But try to explain, using the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I'll show you now the districts in which I participated in ethnic cleansing, so it would be Podhum, Panjevina, Djikovina, then Strelcevina, Avenija. Here on the map, I don't see some areas which are here. And there I also participated in ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, just I would ask you to take the marker and just put numbers on the relevant areas; one, two, three, and give the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number one, what do you mean? Just for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Number one is Zahum. It's this part here, because -- as a matter of fact, I cannot really be very definite here on the map. But it's roughly here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: The second is Panjevina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number three.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Number 3 is Kralja Tvrtka which was called Dum, and then a locality next to the school of medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Number 5 is Avenija, and around Mostarka building

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any specific instructions from your commanders how to treat the Muslims during the cleansing operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: It was very hard. We were to seize the keys to the flats from those Muslims. All of the jewellery, everything valuable they would have around their necks, wrists, fingers, and in case of resistance, we were to trample over them. So some did resist, and they would get the pistol or the rifle on the head and so on and so forth. It's not easy to go back to those old days, so I'd really not elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the property left by the Muslims in their abandoned flats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Baja and some other people took this property away at night. We were not allowed to go back to those districts, to those neighbourhoods one day after the cleansing. But the second day, we could already pick out a flat and start -- and become its owners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the apartments that were abandoned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Some of the flats had been taken by -- were taken by soldiers, by members of Benko Penavic. Some, I think, remained empty, unused, and vacated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told the Trial Chamber that some Muslims were taken to Heliodrom, and some Muslims were forced to go across the confrontation line. Could you just indicate on the map, the same map, the route you personally took Muslim civilians across the confrontation line. If you find it, maybe you'll draw a line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: You mean using the marker?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I've just drawn two lines. This is the first one and this one is the second. On the first one, I would like to explain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: This is a street that went passed the church. And this one here was right next to the front line which we manned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you should put a number 6 on the first line and number 7 on the second line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Muslims wounded or killed during those cleansing operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, this happened on several occasions. While they were being driven to the other side, they were being shot, and after some were beaten and there were -- occasionally we would see dead bodies of a person who had been driven from the western part. I would like to add that the dead bodies of people, after a few days, would turn dark in the sun, and they would swell. So the prisoners from the Heliodrom would have to come in to the open and pull those bodies away so that the stench would be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: There's some confusion going on up here, and perhaps the President could address you on that. We're a little at sea about who this witness is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Shall we go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think we owe it to everybody to say that we have been looking at the wrong summary and that's why we were confused, and we wondered had the names been reversed. We were looking in the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We have witnesses with the same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, for interrupting. But Judge Liu and I were wondering what had happened with your evidence, but we didn't put two and two together and realise that there were two people with exactly the same name giving different evidence. Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, now, let's go to the confrontation line. I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit Number 14.5. That's our traditional exhibit. We use it in every session. You may leave -- the other exhibit you should also leave on the witness desk. Witness, I would like you to take a look at the map and this picture. Are you able to show us the area of your unit's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: It would be this part here, from the intersection up to this green area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may draw a line here indicating just the area of your responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other units on the confrontation line that were in charge of some parts of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were certain units that were in charge for certain sections of the front line. Let me show it to you right away. To the left of us, there was Stela's unit. And from this point here to all the way to Podhum was the 4th Battalion, which was also called Tihomir Misic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just -- I would like you just to put Number 8 on the line indicating your area of responsibility on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And you just told the Trial Chamber that some other part of the confrontation line was run by Stela. Do you mean the same Stela you mentioned in the beginning of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: That was Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And now I would like you to take the picture. Could you show which buildings were occupied by your unit? In which buildings did you keep your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: The position of my unit was exactly here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You may encircle it and put number "1."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: This is an approximation. You cannot see exactly where the buildings are, because now this is all overgrown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And what were your functions on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I was one of those who was selected to do special tasks, either during the attack or defence, during the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "special tasks?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Those special tasks were, if there was an action, to extend this west side of Herceg-Bosna or also during major operations when the ABiH was attacking, we were to be ready and prepared at any time to go wherever it was necessary to go to help out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other tasks were carried out by you on the confrontation line, apart from your main task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I went to the Heliodrom on several occasions and collected prisoners, took them to Blato [phoen] where they were filling bags with sand. And then took them to places where they had to build the fortifications. I was at the front line on several occasions while they were working, and I was guarding them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was authorised to take prisoners from Heliodrom and take them to the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: There was Elvir Sadzak whom I spent some time guarding the prisoners, and there was a man called Zubac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Heliodrom to pick up prisoners yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you inform briefly the Trial Chamber how did the system work. I mean the system of ordering prisoners and taking them and returning them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: It wasn't anything much. It would be just a piece of paper signed by Mario Milicevic Baja, and then we would go to the Heliodrom, and we only had a number of prisoners on that piece of paper, so if indeed the number was 30, then we needed to collect 30 prisoners. On the way back, it was not important whether 30 or 25 would be brought back. They were just Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you normally return prisoners on the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Usually on the same day, but sometimes we would keep them at the base of Benko Penavic, the Rondo, we would keep them in the basement because we would perhaps need them very early the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show the witness Exhibit Number 16.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this picture, the building depicted here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: This is the building that was used as the base of Benko Penavic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you indicate on this picture where did you keep prisoners for the night in case that they were kept on your base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I could show it. It was in a basement of this building. You can see windows, parts of the window here and there. This is where we would spend -- they would spend days and nights. And it was there that they would usually also be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, put number "1" indicating the basement where the prisoners were kept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what kind of job did prisoners perform on the confrontation line? Did they work during the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: They were working in different situations, at different times. It was not important whether there was shooting going on, there was like fierce fighting going on, the prisoners had to work. In fact, they were sometimes exposed to the fire from the east side. In fact, on a number of occasions, they were not allowed to hide -- take cover behind a tree or some sandbags, but rather they had to step out into the open and continue with their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit Number 774, P, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see prisoners being wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I would like to say that as far as woundings are concerned, Mario Milicevic, Baja, was mostly involved with that. He was rarely showing up because it was considered to be too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. While the registrar is looking for the exhibit, just one question about Baja again. Did he ever participate in cleansing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. operations himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, he participated. It was he to whom we needed to hand over the keys to the apartments that we had vacated from Muslims, of Muslims. In fact, on his own, he cleansed a village called Kozica. Based on information I had, this he did on his own initiative, and according to the same information, Tuta had saved that village for public relations purposes so that the public would see that this was not done. But Baja made a mistake and he cleansed it anyway on his own, and then he had to go and report to Tuta about it. I personally talked to Baja after he had spoken to Tuta, but didn't ask him what had happened. And he said that he had received a warning, and Tuta had told him that this was no longer to be done. Whenever there was cleansing or any other decision, that it was he that was to be asked first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if your commander, Mario Milicevic, was punished for disobedience, or for his wrong initiative, I would say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: No, he was never punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What about the exhibit? It has my remarks here. It bears my remarks. Maybe we have it in the binder. I suppose we have it. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one question, one more question about Baja while the usher is preparing the exhibit: And did ever Baja command on the confrontation line while there were some military operations there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did ever Baja participate in the military operations on the confrontation line, giving orders, to be present among his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would like you to open this document. You may look either B/C/S version or the English version. And just number 45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment. Could you go back about 20 lines when you posed a question. I heard something, and the response was another thing, and it doesn't seem to make sense. It was in relation to prisoners being wounded or killed when you asked -- and I thought this witness said that Baja was not involved in that because he was never there, but the transcript says the opposite. I wonder, would you go back and look at that and clarify it, because it's a major difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness AC, you understand that there is some confusion. Maybe you'll be able to clarify the situation. Just, was ever Mario Milicevic involved in some actions on the confrontation line which resulted in wounding or killing of some prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: This is a clearer question. Yes, Baja did take part in some of those actions but, as I said, very rarely. He took part in an action on the Bulevar which was conducted in such a way that from the church, we were to cross over to the building which was next to the police building, and then move on to the Bulevar. The prisoners were exposed to the fire and used as human shields. The prisoners were to come out into the open in the street and put up certain sandbags which would protect that space from certain buildings, from the Bulevar. So the prisoners had to cross over and do this. However, a fire --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AC, slow down. Slow down. It's very important, and we cannot skip your information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: One of the prisoners escaped to the other side on that occasion, while another one was hesitant. He didn't know what to do, whether to run to the east or to go back. Most probably this prisoner would have gone back but had no opportunity. Baja, however, resolved that by shooting him dead right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your unit the only one involved in that military operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which units took part in it, units or unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: In this operation, when this took place, or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which units took part in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: On the scene, there was only our unit. But on our right flank, the 4th Battalion was to also take part. And on our left flank, it was to have been Stela and the others. They were to move the front line forward. At least, that is the information that we received from Baja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see prisoners wounded or killed as a result of that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can't [sic] you tell us approximately when that operation took place, if you can, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, I would like usher -- just, let's finish this part of his testimony relevant to this operation, just not to return to it again, because really I planned to do it somewhere later. But it so happened that the witness told the story on his own initiative, asked by Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue to finish this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Like the witness to be shown Exhibit Number P14.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps, Witness, you remember the part of the confrontation line where that operation took place? Could you show it on the picture -- in the picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I would like to show you this area here. We were approximately here, where this church is, and we were to cross over to this building across the street. Because this whole side, this was east part, that is under the control of the ABiH. We feared that fire could come from those buildings. So the prisoners were supposed to place the sandbags across the street so that we could cross over to Rado Polje, and from there on to these buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could draw a line showing the location where the prisoners were made to carry sandbags and make a sort of fortification.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: That would be about here approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put a number 1. And perhaps you will be able to show the medical centre here in the picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: I'm showing the medical centre right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic, Stela, was in charge of the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could encircle the area of his responsibility as far as you know it. Take a pencil and circle it and put number "2."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: That would be it approximately. It would be this area here. I'm not sure how far down it would extend to, but I am certain about this area at the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, our time is up. Sorry for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I'm afraid we have to keep you here for another day. As I warned to other witnesses, please do not talk to anybody about your testimony today, and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning, we'll sit in the morning session in Courtroom III, which means we'll start at 9.00 in the morning. So we are adjourned until 9.00 tomorrow morning.
